title: Past continuous and pluperfect
seoTitle: Turkish past continuous and pluperfect tenses
intro: This unit gives you the two tenses that every story needs besides the plain past. The past continuous `-(I)yordu` paints the scene, *Yağmur yağıyordu* (It was raining), and the pluperfect `-mIştI` reaches further back, *Film çoktan başlamıştı* (The film had already started). Both are built the same way, a tense plus the past of **to be**, and a handful of adverbs (*o sırada, birden, çoktan*) hold the story together.

blocks.text: Take the [present continuous](gp-present-continuous) and put it in the past with `-DI`: *geliyor* (is coming) → *geliyordu* (was coming). The r of *-yor* is voiced, so the D is always d, and the vowel is always u: *-yordu*, whatever the verb. The endings are type II, the ones of the [past tense](gp-past-di). Turkish grammars call this form *şimdiki zamanın hikâyesi*.

The stem changes exactly as it does before `-(I)yor` in the present: a final a or e narrows (*bekliyordu*, *anlıyordu*), *de-* and *ye-* become *diyordu* and *yiyordu*, and *git-* and *et-* soften to *gidiyordu*, *ediyordu*.

For **they**, the plural usually comes before the past, and the past follows its harmony: *geliyorlardı*. *Geliyordular* is also heard, and with a plural subject the bare *geliyordu* is common: *Çocuklar bahçede oynuyordu* (The children were playing in the garden).
It has three main uses:

items: **The scene.** What the weather was like, what people were doing, while the story happens: *Kar yağıyordu. Sokakta kimse yoktu.* (It was snowing. There was nobody in the street.)

**An interrupted action.** Something was going on when an event, in `-DI`, broke in: *Kitap okuyordum, telefon çaldı.* (I was reading a book when the phone rang.) Turkish simply puts the two clauses side by side.
**A state over a period.** *O zamanlar Ankara'da çalışıyordum.* (At that time I was working in Ankara.) For repeated habits, [B1 unit 2](gp-used-to) adds a more typical form, *çalışırdım*.

items.en: It was raining.

items.tr: Güneş parlıyordu ve hafif bir rüzgâr esiyordu.
items.seg: Güneş parl|ıyor|du ve hafif bir rüzgâr es|iyor|du.
items.en: The sun was shining and a light wind was blowing.
I was cooking when someone knocked at the door.

items.tr: Dün akşam saat sekizde ne yapıyordun?
items.seg: Dün akşam saat sekizde ne yap|ıyor|du|n?
items.en: What were you doing at eight o'clock yesterday evening?
The children were playing in the garden.
Back then we were living in Izmir.

blocks.title: Okudum or okuyordum?
blocks.text: *Dün akşam kitap okudum* tells what you did: **I read a book**, full stop. *Dün akşam kitap okuyordum* puts you in the middle of it: **I was reading a book**, and the listener waits for what happened next.

The past continuous covers much of what the French imparfait does for a scene: *Yağmur yağıyordu*, il pleuvait. For repeated habits, though, Turkish prefers the past aorist of B1 unit 2, *Her yaz köye giderdik* (nous allions au village chaque été), where French uses the imparfait again.
With *neredeyse* (almost), the past continuous tells a near miss: *Neredeyse düşüyordum* (I almost fell). You were on the way to falling, and then you weren't.

Add `-DI` to `-mIş` and you get **had done**: *gelmiş* → *gelmişti* (had come). After ş the D is always t: *-mıştı, -mişti, -muştu, -müştü*, in four-way harmony with the verb. The endings are type II again. Turkish grammars call it *öğrenilen geçmiş zamanın hikâyesi*.
`-mIş` starts with a consonant, so the stem never changes: *gitmişti*, *yemişti*, *demişti*.
Use it for:

items: **An earlier past.** The story is in the past, and this happened before it: *Sinemaya vardık, ama film çoktan başlamıştı.* (We got to the cinema, but the film had long since started.)
**Experience up to a past moment**, often with *daha önce* (before) or *hiç* (ever, never): *O güne kadar hiç deniz görmemiştim.* (I had never seen the sea until that day.)
**Reminding someone** of what was said or done earlier: *Sana söylemiştim!* (I told you so!), *Ne demiştin?* (What did you say? — asking someone to repeat what they said a moment ago).

items.en: The film had already started.
We got to the station, but the train had left.

items.tr: Daha önce hiç Türk kahvesi içmemiştim.
items.seg: Daha önce hiç Türk kahvesi iç|me|miş|ti|m.
items.en: I had never had Turkish coffee before.
I told you so!
Had you had breakfast?
I had left my key at home.

blocks.title: Not hearsay
blocks.text: Despite its `-mIş`, the pluperfect doesn't report hearsay. *Ali gelmişti* is **Ali had come**, something you know; the hearsay of [A2 unit 2](gp-mis-intro) is *Ali gelmiş*, **Ali has come, I hear**. Listen for the *-ti*.

Turkish uses `-mIştI` more freely than English uses **had**. When you point back to an earlier moment, especially to remind someone of it, English often has a plain past where Turkish has the pluperfect: *Bu filmi geçen yıl izlemiştik* (We watched this film last year, remember?).

*Geliyordu* and *gelmişti* are the first two members of a family. Each is a tense suffix, then the past of **to be**, `-(y)DI`, which you put on nouns in [A2 unit 2](gp-past-copula) (*öğrenciydim*), then a type II ending. Turkish grammars call the family *hikâye birleşik zamanı*, the narrative compound.
Four rules cover them all:

items: **The D follows the sound before it**: d after r and vowels (*geliyordu*, *gelirdi*), t after ş and k (*gelmişti*, *gelecekti*). After a vowel the buffer y comes in: *gelmeliydi*.

**In a question, `mI` comes right after the tense suffix** and carries `-(y)DI` and the ending: *geliyor muydun?*, *gelmiş miydi?* That's the pattern of *hasta mıydın?*, not of the simple past *geldin mi?*
**The plural `-lAr` of they comes before `-DI` and before `mI`**: *geliyorlardı*, *gelmişler miydi?*

items.en: Were you asleep at that moment?
Ali wasn't answering the phone.
Had you been to Ankara before?
Had the guests arrived?
Was it snowing yesterday?

blocks.text: Don't move `mI` to the end as in the simple past. *Geldin mi?* (Did you come?) has `mI` last, but *Geliyor muydun?* (Were you coming?) has it in the middle. *Geliyordun mu?* is wrong.

In formal writing the past of **to be** may stand as a separate word, *idi*, as you saw with [idi and imiş](gp-idi-imis): *geliyor idi* = *geliyordu*, *gelmiş idi* = *gelmişti*. In speech and everyday writing, use the suffix.

sections.title: Çoktan, o sırada, birden: holding a story together

blocks.text: A story moves between its scene, its events and what came before. A few adverbs tell the listener which is which, and each has a tense it likes.

head: Word
Meaning
Usually with
rows: long since, a long time ago; already
(with a negative) not yet; (with a positive) just
then, at that time; in that case
suddenly, all of a sudden (a little more written)

blocks.text: **Çoktan** says something happened long before the moment you're talking about: *Ben vardım, ama otobüs çoktan kalkmıştı* (I arrived, but the bus had long since left). With the present it means **already, for ages**: *Ben çoktan hazırım* (I've been ready for ages).

**Henüz** you know from [A2 unit 1](gp-time-past): with a negative, **not yet**, *Saat ondu ama Ali henüz gelmemişti* (It was ten, but Ali hadn't come yet). With a positive verb it means **just**: *Henüz yatmıştım* (I had just gone to bed). In speech, **just** is more often *daha yeni*: *Daha yeni yatmıştım*.

**O sırada** freezes the scene at the moment of an event: *O sırada ben mutfakta çay yapıyordum* (At that moment I was making tea in the kitchen). **Birden** and **aniden** bring in the event that breaks it. **Tam** (exactly), which you met in [A2 unit 9](a2-u09), adds **just as**: *Tam çıkıyordum, telefon çaldı* (I was just leaving when the phone rang).

items.en: I was walking in the street. Suddenly it started to rain.

items.tr: O sırada ben mutfakta çay yapıyordum.
items.seg: O sırada ben mutfakta çay yap|ıyor|du|m.
items.en: At that moment I was making tea in the kitchen.

items.tr: Biz vardık, ama film çoktan bitmişti.
items.seg: Biz var|dı|k, ama film çoktan bit|miş|ti.
items.en: We arrived, but the film had long since finished.

items.tr: Saat ondu ama Ali henüz gelmemişti.
items.seg: Saat on|du ama Ali henüz gel|me|miş|ti.
items.en: It was ten o'clock, but Ali hadn't come yet.
I was just leaving when the phone rang.

blocks.text: Here is a whole story with the three tenses at work: the scene in `-(I)yordu`, the events in `-DI`, and what had happened earlier in `-mIştI`.

blocks.tr:
Geçen kış bir gece eve dönüyordum. Hava çok soğuktu ve kar yağıyordu. Sokakta kimse yoktu. Birden arkamda bir ses duydum. Döndüm ve baktım: küçük bir köpek! Köpek arkamdan geliyordu.

Apartmanın kapısına geldim ve anahtarımı aradım, ama anahtar yoktu: sabah evde unutmuştum. O sırada komşum Elif pencereden bakıyordu. Hemen indi ve kapıyı açtı. Köpek de bizimle içeri girdi.

glossary.en: to follow me, to come along behind me

blocks.title: Three tenses, three jobs
blocks.text: *Kar yağıyordu* (scene) → *Birden bir ses duydum* (event) → *Anahtarı sabah unutmuştum* (earlier). If you change one tense, you change the story: *Kar yağdı* would make the snow an event of its own.

summary: Past continuous: stem + `-(I)yor` + *-du* + type II ending: *geliyordum, geliyordun, geliyordu, geliyorduk, geliyordunuz, geliyorlardı*.
Use it for the scene of a story, an action that something interrupted, and states over a period: *Kitap okuyordum, telefon çaldı.*
Pluperfect: stem + `-mIş` + *-tI* + type II ending: *gelmiştim*. Use it for what had happened before a past moment, and to remind: *Sana söylemiştim!*
*Gelmişti* is **had come**; plain *gelmiş* is hearsay, **has come, I hear**.
Compound tenses keep the negative inside (*gelmiyordum*, *gelmemiştim*) and put `mI` straight after the tense: *geliyor muydun?*, *gelmiş miydi?*
*O sırada* goes with the scene, *birden* and *aniden* with the event that breaks in, *çoktan* with what had long since happened.
